strengths: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of a previously overlooked incompatibility between curriculum learning and aggressive LR decay, with compelling visualizations (Figure 1) showing how curriculum benefits diminish with standard schedules

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple dimensions: systematic ablations on decay parameters (Figure 2), multiple quality metrics (DCLM, PreSelect), multiple datasets (DCLM-Baseline, WebOrganizer), and both single-phase and practical mid-training settings

Multiple complementary solutions proposed with clear characterization: moderate decay alone achieves near-optimal results; weight averaging + constant LR (CMA) achieves comparable performance; combined approach (CDMA) provides synergistic benefits with 1.2-1.68% mid-training improvements
Excellent presentation with logical narrative progression, effective figures, and clear practical implementation details (Algorithm 1) that integrate into existing preprocessing pipelines

Theoretical analysis (Section 6) provides intuitive explanation through simplified quadratic model, explaining why weight averaging maintains update magnitude while reducing noise compared to LR decay

Thorough robustness checks demonstrating generalization: different decay functions produce similar results (Table 4), ablations on alternative metrics and unfiltered datasets, analysis of why prior folding approaches fail at higher LRs
weaknesses: Limited experimental scale (1.5B parameters, 30B tokens) raises generalization concerns; unclear how findings extend to larger models (7B-70B+) where optimal hyperparameters, data scaling laws, and weight averaging dynamics may differ substantially

Theoretical analysis uses oversimplified 2D quadratic model with uniform random noise, creating loose connection to actual neural network training; theory explains why weight averaging + constant LR works but not why moderate decay + averaging (CDMA) is optimal or how it compares across scales

Hyperparameter sensitivity is high: optimal ending LR differs 100× between curriculum (1×10⁻³) and uniform (1×10⁻⁵) ordering, requiring careful tuning; weight averaging parameters (α=0.2, 6 checkpoints) appear arbitrary with limited ablation; 'previously overlooked regime' is discovered through ablation rather than predicted

Inconsistent results on PreSelect metric (Table 6, Figure 8): ascending curriculum shows final validation loss exceeding uniform baseline, attributed to dataset filtering misalignment but raising concerns about metric-agnostic robustness; core score improvements exist but undermined by validation loss issue

High-quality validation set drawn from DCLM-top-10% documents directly aligns with DCLM-ordered curricula, potentially biasing results despite strong downstream correlation; generalization to validation sets from different distributions untested

Mid-training improvements (1.2-1.68%) substantially exceed single-phase improvements (0.38-1.20%), with authors attributing this to sparse high-quality data amplifying per-sample value; this explanation is plausible but not rigorously demonstrated, could reflect specific WebOrganizer+DCLM mixture effects

Somewhat incremental novelty: combines two well-established techniques (curriculum learning, weight averaging) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods; main contribution is identifying their incompatibility and co-optimization, limiting scope

Missing statistical reporting: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or clarification whether reported results are from single runs or averaged across multiple seeds, making small differences difficult to assess

Incomplete analysis of why folding curriculum fails at high LR (Table 9): post-hoc explanation provided but not systematically tested; unexplored whether other data ordering strategies similarly interact with LR schedules
